headline: October 2026 'has emerged as the most intense period of maritime attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the escalation'
dek: Marisks (Greece-based consultancy) told Reuters: 'October 2026 has emerged as the most intense period of maritime attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the escalation of hostilities in March.' UKMTO (British maritime security service) recorded 135 incidents related to the US-Iran…
sources: Marisks (Greece-based maritime consultancy) via Reuters; UKMTO; Times Now market data; Bob McNally (Rapidan Energy)
fault_line: Are the tankers really being hit, or is Tehran taxing fear? Commenters split between 'believe the ports' and 'fear is the weapon' -- and pocketbook rage: $150 oil vs 'small price to pay'

sections.what_happened: Marisks (Greece-based consultancy) told Reuters: 'October 2026 has emerged as the most intense period of maritime attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the escalation of hostilities in March.' UKMTO (British maritime security service) recorded 135 incidents related to the US-Iran conflict as of October 16, and reported a sharp rise in ship damage caused by attacks in October. Brent crude rose as much as 3.8% to $117.45 a barrel during New York trading Friday -- first time above $117 since April -- before settling at $116.72; up more than 10% this month. Bob McNally (Rapidan Energy president): crude could reach about $150/barrel if the conflict escalates and damages critical oil infrastructure.
sections.what_verified: Marisks quote attributed to named consultancy speaking to Reuters (carried by CGTN Oct 24). UKMTO figures come from the service itself (carried by CGTN). Brent levels from Times Now market reporting. McNally quote is analyst projection (Times Now). No independent second witness to Marisks' internal intensity assessment, but it is a named expert attribution, not an anonymous claim.
sections.what_disputed: None to the Marisks/UKMTO intensity verdict in-window. Note: social chatter (single unattributed post, 2026-10-21) claims Gulf oil exports have 'risen above pre-war levels' and Hormuz traffic 'recovered to 82% of normal' -- unattributed, unverified, treat as audience misinformation until a declared-tier source carries it. Bessent's 'surpassed pre-conflict levels' claim (ET, single family) also unverified.
sections.why_matters: October is officially the most violent month in Hormuz since March -- the data says it, not the claims. PortWatch counts the ships that DID move; Marisks counts the ones that got hit. Numbers over narratives.
sections.context: Background: NEW (in-window; Hormuz by the Numbers franchise) -- Marisks to Reuters: October 2026 'has emerged as the most intense period of maritime attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the escalation of hostilities in March'; UKMTO: 135 incidents as of Oct 16, sharp rise in ship damage in October; Brent hit $117.45 Friday (4-year high, settled $116.72); Rapidan's McNally warns $150 if escalation damages critical infrastructure

totw_analysis: Our read: October is officially the most violent month in Hormuz since March -- the data says it, not the claims. PortWatch counts the ships that DID move; Marisks counts the ones that got hit. Numbers over narratives. The fault line our audience is arguing over: Are the tankers really being hit, or is Tehran taxing fear? Commenters split between 'believe the ports' and 'fear is the weapon' -- and pocketbook rage: $150 oil vs 'small price to pay'
